results.result: The authors developed a SHERLOCK4AAT toolbox comprising seven assays targeting different trypanosome species and groups. Target selection was based on conserved regions of the 18S rRNA, IFX, and GAPDH genes, with specificity confirmed through BLAST analysis and sequence alignment showing appropriate conservation within target species and divergence from non-target species.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C24-C31, and C70-C77 collectively demonstrate systematic target selection and validation. The in silico analyses (BLAST, sequence alignments) and specificity testing (Figure 1B-C) provide strong evidence for appropriate target design. The molecular basis for discrimination is well-documented with specific sequence identity percentages and accession numbers.

results.result: The SHERLOCK4AAT assays demonstrated high specificity, with each assay detecting only its intended target species without cross-reactivity to non-target trypanosomes, co-endemic parasites (P. falciparum), or host genetic material.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 and C78 are supported by experimental data in Figures 1B-C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The specificity testing included appropriate positive and negative controls across multiple related species, demonstrating no cross-reactivity. The experimental design is sound with adequate replication (N=3-9).

results.result: The analytical sensitivity (limit of detection) varied across assays: pan-trypanosomatid (10-10³ parasites/ml), pan-Trypanozoon (10 parasites/ml), T. theileri (10 parasites/ml), T. congolense (10-10³ parasites/ml), T. vivax (10⁴-10⁵ parasites/ml), and T. simiae/T. suis (10-100 fM synthetic controls).
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 are supported by serial dilution experiments shown in Figure 2A-B. The LoD determinations follow standard methodology with appropriate controls. However, the T. vivax assay shows notably lower sensitivity (C35, C91), and T. simiae/T. suis were tested only with synthetic controls due to lack of parasite material, which limits confidence in real-world performance.

results.result: Multiplexing two crRNAs in the pan-trypanosomatid assay increased median sensitivity from 66.1% to 74.7% while maintaining specificity above 80%, and improved concordance with pan-Trypanozoon results from 7.8% to 25.7% double positives.
results.evaluation: Claims C37, C79-C80 are supported by Bayesian statistical analysis (Figure 3B) and experimental comparison (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The Monte Carlo method using Gibbs sampling is appropriate for estimating test performance in the absence of a gold standard. The improvement in fold-change readouts at lower dilutions is experimentally demonstrated.

results.result: Positivity thresholds were established for each assay using ROC curve analysis, ranging from 1.546 (T. simiae) to 11.70 (pan-Trypanozoon).
results.evaluation: Claim C38 is supported by ROC curve analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2. The methodology using Youden's index to maximize classification accuracy is statistically sound. Thresholds were selected to achieve 100% specificity, which is appropriate for diagnostic applications.

results.result: The analytical sensitivities of the pan-trypanosomatid, pan-Trypanozoon, T. theileri, and T. congolense SHERLOCK assays were comparable to existing PCR-based molecular tools (1-10 parasites/ml for genus/species-specific primers).
results.evaluation: Claims C89 and C55 are supported by comparison of LoD data (C32-C34) with cited literature values. The comparison is appropriate and shows SHERLOCK performance is within the range of existing methods. However, the advantage of RNA detection (C90) for identifying active infections is stated but not experimentally validated in this study.

results.result: The T. vivax SHERLOCK assay targeting the single-copy IFX gene did not meet sensitivity requirements for molecular diagnosis of animal trypanosomes.
results.evaluation: Claim C91 is supported by the LoD data (C35) showing 10⁴-10⁵ parasites/ml, which is 100-1000× less sensitive than other assays and comparable to microscopy methods (C16). The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation and suggest identifying alternative targets.

results.result: A total of 424 blood samples were collected from domestic pigs: 224 free-ranging pigs in Côte d'Ivoire and 200 farm pigs in Guinea.
results.evaluation: Claims C23, C39-C40 describe the sample collection methodology. The sample sizes are adequate for epidemiological surveillance, and the geographic locations are appropriate for studying HAT foci. The sampling strategy is clearly described in the Methods section.

results.result: High prevalence of trypanosome infections was detected: 74.6% [68.9, 80.3] in Côte d'Ivoire and 49.5% [42.6, 56.9] in Guinea tested positive in at least one SHERLOCK assay, with an overall 62.7% [58.1, 67.3] infection rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C41-C42 are supported by screening data shown in Figures 4B and 5B with appropriate confidence intervals. The high prevalence is consistent with the endemic nature of the study areas. Statistical reporting is appropriate with 95% confidence intervals calculated using the Wilson/Brown method.

results.result: Species-specific prevalence varied between sites: multiplex pan-trypanosomatid detected 41.1% in Côte d'Ivoire and 29.5% in Guinea; pan-Trypanozoon detected ~38-39% in both countries; T. congolense was found in 23.2% in Côte d'Ivoire but only 7.5% in Guinea.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48, C50-C51 are supported by quantitative data with confidence intervals shown in Figures 4C and 5C. The geographic differences in T. congolense prevalence are notable and appropriately reported. The data are consistent with known epidemiology of these parasites.

results.result: T. b. gambiense was detected in one pig at each site, representing a low prevalence of 0.45 ± 0.9% in Côte d'Ivoire and 0.50 ± 1.0% in Guinea.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C49, C61 are supported by screening data (Figures 4B, 5B). The low prevalence is accurately calculated and reported with uncertainty estimates. However, the characterization of one positive sample in Côte d'Ivoire is concerning as it was negative in all other assays and parasitological tests (C81), raising questions about false positivity.

results.result: No T. vivax or T. theileri infections were detected in pigs from either study site, confirming that pigs are not frequent carriers of these species.
results.evaluation: Claims C53 and C96 report negative findings. While the absence of detection is clearly stated, this could reflect either true absence or the poor sensitivity of the T. vivax assay (C91, LoD 10⁴-10⁵ parasites/ml). The inference that pigs are not frequent carriers (C96) is supported by citation but the current data cannot distinguish between low prevalence and assay insensitivity.

results.result: Co-infections with Trypanozoon species and T. congolense were common, detected in 15.2% [10.5, 19.9] of samples in Côte d'Ivoire, including 11.0 ± 4.1% triple-positive (pan-trypanosomatid, pan-Trypanozoon, T. congolense) and 4.1 ± 2.6% double-positive (pan-Trypanozoon, T. congolense).
results.evaluation: Claims C54, C83-C87 are supported by data shown in Figures 4D and 5D. The identification of co-infections demonstrates the value of the multi-assay approach. The inference that triple-positive results indicate co-infection with T. b. brucei and T. congolense (C85, C87) is reasonable given the assay specificities, though direct species confirmation would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: SHERLOCK4AAT assays showed comparable or superior sensitivity to combined parasitological methods (median sensitivity 91.4% vs 84.3%) while maintaining specificity above 75%, based on comparison with buffy coat examination, mAECT, and mouse isolation in Côte d'Ivoire samples.
results.evaluation: Claims C44 and C43 are supported by Bayesian latent class modeling shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The statistical approach is appropriate for comparing tests without a gold standard. The higher detection rate by SHERLOCK (74.6%) versus parasitology (47.3%) is consistent with the sensitivity estimates. However, parasitological data were not available for Guinea samples, limiting generalizability.

results.result: Domestic pigs do not likely represent a significant risk to gHAT elimination given the low T. b. gambiense prevalence (0.45-0.50%), short commercial lifespan (6-8 months), absence of new human cases, and low tsetse abundance.
results.evaluation: Claims C63, C61-C62, C103 make an important public health inference. While the low prevalence (C61) and short lifespan (C62) are factual, the conclusion relies on unpublished data about human cases and tsetse abundance (C103). The inference also doesn't account for potential transmission dynamics, the possibility of higher prevalence in other pig populations, or the role of other animal reservoirs. This conclusion requires more comprehensive epidemiological modeling.

results.result: Pigs could serve as sentinels to monitor T. b. gambiense circulation using SHERLOCK4AAT due to their proximity to humans, attractiveness to tsetse flies, and demonstrated ability to carry human-infective trypanosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C97, C104 propose pigs as sentinel animals. While the detection of T. b. gambiense in pigs (C5, C49) demonstrates feasibility, and pig characteristics (proximity to humans, tsetse attractiveness) are cited (C104, C67), this remains speculative. The very low prevalence (0.45-0.50%) would require large sample sizes for effective surveillance. The proposal lacks cost-effectiveness analysis or comparison with alternative surveillance strategies.

results.result: SHERLOCK4AAT assays can be run in 2.5 hours at €2.5 per test, are optimized for high-throughput fluorescence screening in standard lab conditions, and are intended for eco-epidemiological surveillance rather than field diagnosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C56, C93, C57 describe practical characteristics of the assays. The time and cost estimates are clearly stated, and the technical requirements (fluorescence reader, basic molecular biology training) are appropriate for the described application. The authors appropriately acknowledge that the current version is not suitable for point-of-care field diagnosis (C57), though they suggest future development in this direction (C102).

results.result: The SHERLOCK4AAT results from Côte d'Ivoire (37.9% Trypanozoon, 23.2% T. congolense) are consistent with previous PCR studies (57% Trypanozoon, 24% T. congolense), confirming the effectiveness of the toolbox for analyzing trypanosome distribution in hypo-endemic gHAT foci.
results.evaluation: Claims C94, C60, C100 compare current results with prior studies. The T. congolense prevalence is remarkably consistent (23.2% vs 24%), while Trypanozoon detection is lower (37.9% vs 57%). This difference could reflect the different assay sensitivities or true epidemiological changes. The consistency for T. congolense and the species discrimination capability support the effectiveness claim, though the lower Trypanozoon detection warrants discussion.

results.result: Uncharacterized trypanosome species may be circulating in these pig populations, detectable only by the broad multiplex pan-trypanosomatid assay.
results.evaluation: Claim C99 is speculative, based on samples positive only in the multiplex pan-trypanosomatid assay (8.7% in Côte d'Ivoire, 9.5% in Guinea). While this hypothesis is plausible and supported by citation to similar findings in other hosts (Votýpka et al., 2022), alternative explanations include differential assay sensitivities or detection of known species at low parasite loads. Sequencing of these samples would be needed to confirm novel species.

results.result: The two T. b. gambiense-positive samples showed different patterns: the Côte d'Ivoire sample was negative in all other assays and parasitological tests, while the Guinea sample was positive in multiplex pan-trypanosomatid, CATT, and mAECT but negative in pan-Trypanozoon.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 describe discordant results that raise important questions about assay performance and interpretation. The Côte d'Ivoire sample's isolation as TgsGP-positive only (C81) is concerning and could represent a false positive, low-level infection, or assay-specific detection. The Guinea sample's pattern (C82) is more consistent with true infection. These discordances highlight the need for confirmatory testing and careful interpretation of single-assay positives.

results.result: The SHERLOCK4AAT toolbox was developed with seven assays targeting different trypanosome species and groups. The assays include pan-trypanosomatid, pan-Trypanozoon, and species-specific assays for T. vivax, T. congolense, T. theileri, T. simiae, and T. suis, based on conserved and species-specific regions of the 18S rRNA, GAPDH, and IFX genes. Specificity testing showed that each assay detected only its intended target(s) with no cross-reactivity.
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirmed the successful development and specificity of the assays. Reviewer 1 noted 'comprehensive validation' and that the assays 'convincingly allow for the analysis and detection of most trypanosomes in AAT.' Reviewer 3 confirmed the assays 'were able to discriminate between' the target species. The evidence supporting conclusions is described as 'convincing' by the editor.

results.result: The analytical sensitivity (limit of detection) varied across assays: pan-trypanosomatid (10-10³ parasites/ml), pan-Trypanozoon (10 parasites/ml), T. theileri (10 parasites/ml), T. congolense (10-10³ parasites/ml), T. vivax (10⁴-10⁵ parasites/ml), and T. simiae and T. suis (10-100 fM synthetic controls). The authors claim these sensitivities are comparable to existing PCR-based molecular tools.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 identified a major weakness: 'The assay for one key parasite species (T. vivax) shows suboptimal sensitivity, which may limit its utility in detecting this important pathogen.' Reviewer 3 noted the 'IFX gene not achieving the sensitivity requirements for detection of T. vivax' and stated 'Both T. brucei brucei and T. vivax are the most predominant infective species in animals...therefore a reliable assay should be able to convincingly detect these.' While most assays showed acceptable sensitivity, the T. vivax limitation is a significant concern.

results.result: The T. vivax SHERLOCK assay, targeting the single-copy IFX gene, did not meet the sensitivity requirements for molecular diagnosis of animal trypanosomes and would require identification of another target.
results.evaluation: This limitation is explicitly acknowledged by the authors and confirmed by reviewers. Reviewer 1 stated the T. vivax assay 'shows suboptimal sensitivity' and Reviewer 3 noted 'the IFX gene not achieving the sensitivity requirements for detection of T. vivax.' The reviewers treat this as a recognized weakness rather than disputing the authors' assessment.

results.result: The pan-Trypanozoon assay can detect members of the Trypanozoon subgenus (T. b. brucei, T. b. gambiense, T. b. rhodesiense, T. evansi, T. equiperdum) but cannot distinguish between these closely related species. Samples positive for pan-Trypanozoon but negative for T. b. gambiense-specific assay were presumed to be T. b. brucei infections.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 identified this as a major weakness: 'The current assay design does not distinguish between closely related species within the same subgenus—an important factor for certain epidemiological studies.' Reviewer 3 noted the 'Inability for the assay to distinguish T. b. brucei, T. evansi and T. equiperdum using the 18S rRNA gene.' While the assay functions as designed, its inability to differentiate within the subgenus limits its epidemiological utility.

results.result: Multiplexing crRNAs in the pan-trypanosomatid assay increased median sensitivity from 66.1% to 74.7% while maintaining specificity above 80%. The multiplexed version showed improved performance especially at lower parasite concentrations and higher concordance with the pan-Trypanozoon assay (25.7% vs 7.8% double positives).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted the 'robust' methodology and 'comprehensive validation, including statistical analyses to determine sensitivity and specificity.' The editor stated 'The evidence supporting the conclusions is convincing and in line with the current state-of-the-art diagnostics.' No reviewer challenged the multiplexing improvement data.

results.result: Field testing of 424 pig blood samples from Côte d'Ivoire and Guinea revealed high trypanosome infection rates: 62.7% overall infected with at least one species, with 74.6% positive in Côte d'Ivoire and 49.5% in Guinea. Species-specific prevalences included pan-Trypanozoon (38-39%), T. congolense (7.5-23.2%), and multiplex pan-trypanosomatid (29.5-41.1%).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated the authors 'demonstrated field utility through large-scale testing of 424 samples from two geographically distinct regions' and noted 'high infection rates (62.7% of pigs infected).' Reviewer 2 affirmed 'The strength of the evidence is compelling' and praised 'Identification of various sub-species of Trypanosomes.' The editor confirmed the evidence is 'convincing.'

results.result: T. b. gambiense was detected in one pig sample at each site (prevalence 0.45-0.50%), providing evidence that pigs can carry human-infective trypanosomes and act as potential reservoirs. However, the authors conclude these animals do not likely represent a significant risk to gHAT elimination given the low prevalence and short pig life expectancy (6-8 months).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 emphasized this as a major strength: 'The detection of human-infective parasites in pigs at both sites provides important One Health insights' and has 'direct implications for public health policy and disease elimination programs.' Reviewer 2 highlighted 'Differentiating the animal sub-species from the human one' as a strength. Reviewer 3 noted the assays 'convincingly allow for the analysis and detection of most trypanosomes.' The low prevalence finding and risk assessment are accepted without challenge.

results.result: Bayesian statistical analysis suggested that the combination of SHERLOCK4AAT assays may compete with combined parasitological methods in terms of sensitivity (median 91.4% vs 84.3%) while maintaining median specificity above 75%.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted the 'robust' methodology 'incorporating Bayesian statistical modeling' and stated the authors 'conducted comprehensive validation, including statistical analyses to determine sensitivity and specificity.' The comparative analysis with parasitological methods was not challenged by any reviewer.

results.result: Co-infections with Trypanozoon species (likely T. b. brucei) and T. congolense were detected in 15.2% of samples from Côte d'Ivoire and 6.5% from Guinea, based on triple-positive results in pan-trypanosomatid, pan-Trypanozoon, and T. congolense-specific assays.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated 'The findings enhance our understanding of parasite diversity in livestock' and noted the study provides evidence of co-infections. Reviewer 3 confirmed the assays 'convincingly allow for the analysis and detection of most trypanosomes in AAT.' The co-infection data were not questioned by reviewers.

results.result: Each SHERLOCK4AAT assay can be run in 2 hr 30 min at 2.5 € per test (excluding sample processing). All tests are optimized for high-throughput screening with fluorescence readout and can be performed in standard lab conditions by technicians trained in basic molecular biology.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted the 'clear practical advantages such as dried blood spot compatibility' and that the 'revised manuscript also addresses implementation considerations, including cost, training needs, and field logistics.' The practical characteristics were affirmed as strengths for 'resource-limited settings through a short assay duration.'

results.result: The authors suggest that pigs could act as sentinels to monitor T. b. gambiense circulation using SHERLOCK4AAT, given their proximity to humans, attractiveness to tsetse flies, and status as likely underestimated reservoirs of human-infective parasites.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated this provides 'important One Health insights supporting integrated disease surveillance' with 'direct implications for public health policy and disease elimination programs.' The reviewer noted this supports 'One Health strategies and targeted disease elimination efforts.' Reviewer 2 affirmed the significance of 'Differentiating the animal sub-species from the human one.' The sentinel concept is treated as a valuable application.

results.result: T. simiae and T. suis assays were validated using synthetic controls (no biological material available) and showed LoD of 10-100 fM, far from SHERLOCK's theoretical detection capacity of 2 aM for synthetic targets under optimal conditions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 identified this as a weakness: 'some assays relied on synthetic controls due to unavailable biological material.' While the synthetic control validation is not directly challenged, the reliance on synthetic rather than biological validation and the gap between achieved and theoretical sensitivity represents a limitation acknowledged by reviewers.

results.result: No T. vivax or T. theileri RNA was detected in any pig samples from either study site, confirming that pigs are not frequent carriers of these species.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 noted that 'Both T. brucei brucei and T. vivax are the most predominant infective species in animals (in addition to T. congolense)' but did not challenge the negative findings in pigs. The absence of these species in pig samples is consistent with known host preferences and was not disputed.

results.result: A significant advantage of SHERLOCK4AAT is that it detects RNA rather than DNA, probing for active infections rather than persistent nucleic acids that may remain after treatment or in non-blood tissues.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted the methodology offers 'clear practical advantages' including 'detection of active infections.' The RNA-based detection is treated as an advantage over DNA-based methods, particularly given the known persistence of trypanosome DNA after treatment.

results.result: SHERLOCK4AAT was developed for eco-epidemiological surveillance at large scale rather than direct field diagnosis. The authors suggest future development of multiplexed assays with lateral flow tests would be desirable for field-applicable point-of-care versions, and that applying SHERLOCK to skin samples could be useful for monitoring both blood and skin-dwelling parasites.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted 'While certain performance limitations may restrict broader adoption' and that the system 'offers practical benefits for resource-limited settings.' The reviewer acknowledged the current version is not field-ready but represents 'a significant step toward improved disease monitoring.' The future development suggestions are treated as reasonable next steps rather than current limitations.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the systematic target selection and validation (C3, C24-C31, C70-C77). OpenEval emphasizes in silico analyses and specificity testing with sequence data. Peer reviewers affirm 'comprehensive validation' and 'convincing' discrimination between species. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED with high agreement.

OpenEval R2 focuses on specificity testing (C29-C31, C78) with positive/negative controls and finds evidence SUPPORTED. Peer R1 covers overlapping claims (C29-C31) as part of broader validation and also finds them SUPPORTED. Both agree on successful specificity demonstration.

Both address LoD determinations (C32-C36, C89). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED but notes T. vivax limitation and synthetic control concerns. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, identifying 'suboptimal sensitivity' for T. vivax as a 'major weakness' and noting reliance on synthetic controls. Peer review is more critical of these limitations.

Perfect agreement on C91. Both SUPPORT the acknowledgment that T. vivax assay shows poor sensitivity (10⁴-10⁵ parasites/ml). OpenEval notes it's 100-1000× less sensitive than other assays. Peer reviewers confirm this as a recognized weakness without disputing the authors' assessment.

Perfect agreement on C37, C79-C80. Both SUPPORT the multiplexing improvement claims. OpenEval emphasizes Bayesian statistical methodology and experimental validation. Peer reviewers note 'robust' methodology and 'comprehensive validation' with no challenges to the multiplexing data.

Both address prevalence findings (C4, C41-C42). OpenEval R9 focuses on these specific claims and finds them SUPPORTED. Peer R6 covers broader field utility including these claims plus species-specific prevalence (C45-C51), also SUPPORTED. Both affirm high infection rates and field demonstration as strengths.

OpenEval R10 addresses species-specific prevalence data (C45-C48, C50-C51) and finds them SUPPORTED. Peer R6 includes these claims in broader field utility assessment, also SUPPORTED. Both emphasize geographic differences and compelling evidence from large-scale testing.

Both address T. b. gambiense detection in pigs (C5, C49, C61). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED but raises concern about one discordant sample and rates public health inference (C63, C97) as UNCERTAIN. Peer reviewers SUPPORT the findings and emphasize 'important One Health insights' with 'direct implications for public health policy' without expressing uncertainty about the risk assessment.

OpenEval R15 addresses public health inference (C63, C61-C62, C103) and rates it UNCERTAIN due to reliance on unpublished data and lack of comprehensive epidemiological modeling. Peer R7 covers overlapping claims (C63, C97) and finds them SUPPORTED, treating the low prevalence finding and One Health implications as valuable contributions. Significant disagreement on certainty of public health conclusions.

Both address comparative performance with parasitology (C44). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, noting appropriate Bayesian methodology and higher SHERLOCK detection rate (74.6% vs 47.3%). Peer reviewers also SUPPORT, affirming 'robust' methodology with Bayesian modeling. Strong agreement on statistical approach and comparative findings.

Perfect agreement on co-infection detection (C54, C83-C87). Both SUPPORT the findings. OpenEval notes the value of multi-assay approach and reasonable inference about triple-positive results. Peer reviewers affirm enhanced understanding of parasite diversity and convincing detection capabilities.

Both address practical characteristics (C56, C93). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, noting time/cost estimates and appropriate acknowledgment that current version isn't field-ready (C57). Peer reviewers also SUPPORT, emphasizing 'clear practical advantages' including dried blood spot compatibility and suitability for resource-limited settings.

Both address sentinel animal concept (C7, C97, C104). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting very low prevalence would require large sample sizes and lacks cost-effectiveness analysis. Peer reviewers SUPPORT the concept, emphasizing 'important One Health insights' with 'direct implications for public health policy.' Significant disagreement on feasibility and value of sentinel surveillance.

Perfect agreement on C53, C96 (absence of T. simiae/T. suis in pigs). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to poor T. vivax assay sensitivity making it difficult to distinguish true absence from detection failure. Peer reviewers SUPPORT the negative findings without expressing concern about assay sensitivity limitations affecting interpretation.

Both address synthetic control validation (C36, C92). OpenEval R3 notes T. simiae/T. suis tested only with synthetic controls as a limitation but still rates overall LoD claims SUPPORTED. Peer R12 rates UNCERTAIN, identifying reliance on synthetic controls as a weakness. Peer review more critical of this limitation.

OpenEval R6 addresses LoD comparison with literature (C89, C55) and RNA detection advantage (C90), rating SUPPORTED but noting C90 lacks experimental validation. Peer R14 addresses only C90, rating it SUPPORTED and treating RNA-based detection as a clear advantage. Peer review less critical of lack of experimental validation for active infection claims.

Both address current limitations and future development (C57, C66, C101-C102). OpenEval R17 finds practical characteristics SUPPORTED and appropriately acknowledges current version isn't field-ready. Peer R15 also SUPPORTS, noting performance limitations but treating the work as 'a significant step toward improved disease monitoring' with reasonable future development suggestions.

OpenEval R2 addresses specificity testing (C29-C31, C78) and finds SUPPORTED. Peer R4 addresses inability to distinguish within Trypanozoon subgenus (C27, C30, C88) and rates UNCERTAIN, identifying this as a 'major weakness' for epidemiological studies. Different focus: OpenEval on achieved specificity, peer review on limitations of species discrimination.

OpenEval R5 addresses ROC curve analysis and threshold selection (C38) using Youden's index, finding the methodology SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these statistical methods for threshold determination.

OpenEval R8 addresses sample collection methodology (C23, C39-C40), finding adequate sample sizes and appropriate geographic locations, rated SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses sampling methodology.

OpenEval R18 compares current results with prior studies (C94, C60, C100), noting consistency for T. congolense (23.2% vs 24%) but lower Trypanozoon detection (37.9% vs 57%), rated SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these historical comparisons.

OpenEval R19 addresses hypothesis about novel trypanosomatid species (C99) based on pan-assay-only positive samples, rating UNCERTAIN and noting need for sequencing confirmation. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses this speculative finding.

OpenEval R20 addresses discordant results (C81-C82) including concerning single-assay positives that could represent false positives or low-level infections, rated SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically discusses these discordant samples.
